TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
      Save Our Salado (“SOS”) and Supporting Intervenors timely ﬁle this Initial Post-
Hearing Brief.

                                  I. Introduction

       We are the Save Our Salado Intervenor Group. We are a group of over 70
intervenors who live in Salado and are concerned about Link E12. We observed the
proceedings remotely and have many thoughts we wish to share with all y’all honors.
       We, by choice, live in the beautiful village community of Salado. It is a quiet village
with spirit and love. We come here from diﬀerent backgrounds and experiences, and we
represent a good blend, or a microcosm, of the study area. We all share American values
and Texas values: Family, friends and neighbors, health, schools for good education, the
environment, and of course, our wallets or pocketbooks.

       This is our beautiful brief.




                                              4
        We are husbands and wives, sisters and brothers, aunts and uncles, and friends and
neighbors. We are not legal professionals. We are fortunate that we had a small subset of
our neighbors hire Bayliﬀ Law Firm. Brad and his wife have helped educate us on the
procedural steps and they have provided us administrative assistance.




                          Save Our Salado; Initial Post-Hearing Brief
                                           5 of 46
         We, like all the other intervenors in this case, are here to say, “Leave us alone!”
We understand that a selection will be made to someone’s detriment and we regret that is
the typical result of these PUC proceedings.
        Because of the accelerated time schedule, we have had to learn a lot and learn it
fast. We have educated ourselves on routing criteria. We have learned about prudent
avoidance. We have read many studies about the eﬀects of EMFs from transmission lines.
We dove into environmental factors and cultural and historical sites surrounding us.
We have looked at the time, money, and expense that these projects are costing now and
will cost us as ratepayers in the future.
        Our designated contact built a website to organize the group’s concerns. We met
in school facilities, in our homes, at the grocery store, the barber shop, and Salado school
games, exchanging hundreds of emails, texts, and calls to inform ourselves and one
another. So while you, the ALJs in the matter, never saw us physically in the live hearing,
all week during the hearing we were watching, learning, listening and caring.
        We understand that no single factor decides the route-selection question, and that
the Commission has to weigh the criteria in PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC
§ 25.101(b)(3)(B) against the record as a whole. We do not ask the Commission to choose
a route by counting objections or by treating Salado as uniquely exempt from the burdens
of transmission infrastructure. Every route aﬀects someone. The question is whether the
record supports imposing Link E12’s speciﬁc concentrated and avoidable impacts on this
part of Salado when there are supported routes that avoid E12 and better match the route-
wide requirements.
        Link E12 is not merely unpopular. The record reveals it as a link whose apparent
routing proﬁle understates its real-world burden. Nicole Segal’s testimony identiﬁes
organized public concern, missing or understated habitable-structure impacts, and
speciﬁc ways that Link E12 would aﬀect existing homes and people in the Salado Heights
and Golden Eagle area.1 Brenda Holder’s testimony shows the same problem at the parcel
level: Link E12 would not merely cross her family property, it is carelessly positioned to
run lengthwise on a tract, removing the trees and privacy that deﬁne the home. 2 These are
not generalized complaints that transmission lines are undesirable, they are objective facts
showing that the route materials do not fully capture the relevant impact of Link E12.
        Michael Novotny, Superintendent of Salado ISD, explains the school-centered
community impacts of placing a 765-kV line near Salado’s school complex and related

Smith, and Rita Zbranek describe speciﬁc medically vulnerable residents, and identify
related health and prudent-avoidance concerns. 4 Craig and Carleen Edwards explain that
their concerns are not hypothetical, and are based on their own reality of losing their prior

supported by the history of Tenroc Ranch’s recognized land stewardship, shows that
Link E12 would aﬀect land that has been actively restored and managed for decades. 6
Stagecoach Inn and Salado’s historic witnesses explain why the creek-centered, historic,
and tourism character of Salado is a community value. 7
        We do not ask the Commission to resolve disputed medical causation, assign
controlling weight to public opposition, or treat every lay concern as dispositive, in order
to reject Link E12. The SOS testimony has a limited and useful purpose. It supplies
relevant information that is missing from the route tables, including existing homes,
school facilities, narrow parcels, mature trees, restored ranchland, creek corridors, and
historic viewsheds.
        Route 894 provides the practical answer. The Applicants identiﬁed Route 894
as the route that best addresses the Commission’s routing criteria, and Brian Andrews
independently supports Route 894. Route 894 is a Middle route that uses Link C5 and
avoids Link E12, and, because the Northern links are interdependent, it avoids E11, E6,
E7, and E13 as well. SOS therefore supports Route 894, or another route that avoids E12.
When the technical route evidence and the SOS ground-level testimony are considered
together, the balance weighs against any route using Link E12.

                                 II. Summary of Argument

        SOS does not ask the Commission to select a route by sympathy, to count
objections, or to declare Salado immune from infrastructure. Instead, SOS argues that
Link E12 is a short segment whose route-level proﬁle materially understates its actual
burden. The SOS testimony is ground-truth evidence showing that the objective reality
of Link E12’s eﬀect has been understated on many issues that are necessary for a proper
route-wide statutory analysis, including homes, school facilities, medical vulnerabilities,

that makes Salado a community rather than a coordinate on a map.
         The Applicants selected Route 894 as the route that best addresses the
Commission’s routing criteria, and Mr. Andrews independently supports Route 894.
Route 894 avoids E12. The testimony of the SOS witnesses, in real-life terms, shows the
deﬁciencies in much of the previous analysis of Link E12.
         Nicole Segal’s testimony shows that SOS opposition to E12 is not a scattered
collection of preferences; it is correctly framed as a community response containing
information that is essential to the Commission’s decision. Her testimony supplies a
bridge from story to proof by identifying missing or understated habitable-structure
impacts that should have been veriﬁed and cited precisely.8
         Salado ISD shows that E12/E13 concerns are not limited to private landowners.
The district testimony identiﬁes schools and associated athletic and performing-arts
facilities near the proposed links, and places children, parents, staﬀ, and daily school
routines at the center of the routing analysis.9
         The SOS witnesses show that E12 concentrates a set of avoidable burdens, which
may have otherwise passed under the radar, that the Commission can evaluate under the
routing criteria: Ciano and Autrey for health and vulnerable residents; Holder, Smith,
and the Edwardses for homes, proximity, parcel-speciﬁc harm, and safety; Zbranek, Seib
or Bullock, and Cornett for heritage land, creek corridors, ranch stewardship, and land
restoration; and Carrico/Stagecoach Inn for historic Salado and tourism. 10
         This testimony shows that E12 is a link where the route tables do not tell the whole
relevant story. Because Route 894 avoids E12 and is already supported by the Applicants
and Mr. Andrews, and other routing experts who recommend the C5 option to pass
through Bell County, the Commission has a record-supported way to avoid these
concentrated Salado impacts.

the ALJ a list of issues or areas to be addressed in any proceeding referred to SOAH.

        Scope of Brief. This brief focuses on the contested route issues, related cost
issues, and the preliminary-order issues bearing on whether the Commission should reject
routes using Link E12 and approve Route 894 or another non-E12 route. All other issues
identiﬁed in the Order of Referral and Preliminary Order are not separately briefed unless

habitable-structure-data points (Issue Nos. 2–3) are addressed only insofar as they bear on
the accuracy of the record’s route comparison, and not as independent grounds for relief.

           A. Application (Issue No. 1)

           As stated in the Scope of Brief, this issue is not separately briefed.

           B. Notice (Issue Nos. 2-3)

         SOS does not contend that any notice defect requires dismissal or restarting the
docket. SOS raises notice only because the same gaps that aﬀected notice also show that
the route materials do not fully capture who and what Link E12 would aﬀect.
         Craig and Carleen Edwards testify that despite having lived at their home for
nearly a year, they received no oﬃcial notice of the easement behind their home and that
their home does not appear on the transmission-line maps or the habitable-structure list.
Nicole Segal corroborates the omission, testifying that two of the ﬁve houses on her block,
including the home directly next to hers, were left oﬀ the habitable-structure data. These
omissions are relevant to routing: a route whose underlying data misses existing homes
understates E12’s real-world burden, which is the concern that prudent avoidance policies
exist to address.

           C. Public Input (Issue No. 4)

        To the extent this issue is raised, it is to demonstrate the ways public input brings
relevant information to light and bears on the route-comparison and community-values
issues discussed below. SOS does not ask the Commission to treat public input as a vote
count; SOS uses testimony as evidence of ground-level route impacts.

        E. Route (Issue Nos. 8-10)

         The Save Our Salado group all live in Bell County. There are three primary routes
in this case, moving from East to West. The Southern routes use Link B3. The Middle
routes use Link C5, the family to which Route 894 belongs. The Northern routes use Link
E11 and then either Link E6 or Link E12; these Northern links are interdependent,
because neither E6 nor E12 can be reached without ﬁrst using E11, and Links E7 and E13
can be reached only by way of E12.

       This is our roadmap to travel through Bell County.




      The Southern routes: Because they are a bit longer, they are more costly. The
Southern routes also edge closer to Williamson County and get into the urban sprawl of
Metro Austin. No routing expert advocated the use of a Southern route.



                           Save Our Salado; Initial Post-Hearing Brief
                                            10 of 46
         The Middle routes: Seven of eight routes of interest use the Middle route option,
thus, the multi-colored ribbon beginning at Bell County East and using Link C5 westerly
through Bell County to the junction of Bell, Williamson, and Burnet Counties. The
routing experts convincingly conclude, having examined all of the data, that the Middle
route option is the right combination of cost and number of habitable structures.
        The only expert or intervenor testimony that does not recommend the Middle
routes through Bell County comes from parties who own property on the best meets
route. We are sympathetic to them and their situation. We listened to their concerns, but
we do not believe they brought probative issues to this case that exceed those presented by
Links E11, E6, E12: they have beautiful ranches with respected stewardship, and housing
developments in the early planning stages. The Northern routes have these as well.
        The Northern routes: They contain the outliers in the entire study area. The two
links containing the most habitable structures are in the Northern routes, Link E6 and
E12. Because these Northern links are interdependent, a single routing choice resolves
them all: Route 894, a Middle route using Link C5, uses none of them, not E11, E6, E12,
E7, or E13, and so avoids the Northern impact corridor.
        Finally, in addition to the Northern routes containing the highest concentration of
population, they are the closest to the newly-constructed Salado school facilities, and the
closest to the quaint village of Salado, whose economy relies heavily on cultural activities,
historic foundation, and tourism.
        Section 37.056 of PURA sets out factors the Commission must consider in
deciding whether to grant a CCN application. 12 The Commission’s rules add additional
factors governing the routing of transmission lines. While we understand that no route is
better than every other route in every way, Route 894 best meets the criteria of PURA and
the Commission’s rules, especially when the Applicants’ route-selection evidence,
Andrews’s analysis, and the SOS testimony are considered together. 13
        Applicants identiﬁed Route 894 as the route that best addresses the Commission’s
routing criteria. Andrews independently reviewed the Application, EA, ﬁled route data,
testimony/RFIs, and GIS data, and agreed that Route 894 best addresses PURA and the
PUC Substantive Rule. 14

            1.      PURA § 37.056(c)(4) criteria

        Under PURA § 37.056(c)(4), the Commission must consider community values,
recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and
the probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to consumers. Those factors
support rejecting routes that use Link E12 and approving Route 894 or another non-E12
route.

            Community values
         The Commission has described community values as a shared appreciation of an
area or other natural resource by members of a national, regional, or local community.
Adverse eﬀects on community values include those aspects of a proposed project that
would signiﬁcantly alter the use, enjoyment, or intrinsic value attached to an important
area or resource by a community.15 The Commission should evaluate asserted community
values on the evidentiary record and in the context of the other statutory and rule factors.
         Objection to being burdened by a transmission line is not, by itself, a community
value. Landowners understandably oppose lines near their homes and properties, and
every route aﬀects someone. The SOS testimonies show a shared community response to
a link that would pass through established residential areas, near the Salado ISD school
complex, along the Salado Creek corridor, mature trees, long-stewarded land, and near
historic Salado. 16 Salado ISD Superintendent Michael Novotny’s testimony adds an
institutional community-value anchor: the school district and its facilities. 17 Carrico and

            Historical and aesthetic values
        Historical and aesthetic values weigh against routes using Link E12. Hodge and
Segal describe Salado as one of Texas’s most historic towns, the Chisholm Trail running
through downtown along Main Street, and more than forty National Register and
Recorded Texas Historic Landmark sites supporting local businesses, arts, and tourism.21

testimony. 22 The Stagecoach Inn and Salado’s historic core are not merely private
aesthetic preferences. They are part of the setting that supports Salado’s tourism
economy and community identity, and a 765-kV line near that setting is therefore relevant
under PURA’s historical and aesthetic values factor.
        The SOS land witnesses also add aesthetic evidence with speciﬁc land-use
context: Holder’s live oaks, Seib’s heritage oaks, Zbranek’s creek and family land, and
Cornett’s restored ranch landscape. 23 These are not generalized complaints, they are
testimony about how E12 would alter speciﬁc visual and historical settings within Salado
and its surrounding properties.

             Environmental Integrity
         Environmental integrity also supports rejecting E12. The SOS testimonies identify
Salado Creek as a spring-fed Hill Country resource valued for water quality, wildlife
habitat, and recreation. The testimony shows how Link E12 crosses Salado Creek multiple
times.24
         Zbranek, Seib, Bullock, Holder, and Cornett provide important environmental and
land-stewardship testimony. These accounts concern creek corridors, live oaks, heritage
trees, wildlife, native grasses, ranch restoration, water resources, and the disturbance that
would accompany construction and long-term maintenance of a 765-kV corridor. 25 Their
testimony is not limited to private preference or aesthetics. It describes existing land uses
and natural resources that have been preserved, restored, and actively stewarded over
time.
         Zbranek’s testimony shows how Link E12 is tied to Salado Creek and Watkins
Branch. Her family property includes creek frontage, spring-fed water, mature trees,
wildlife habitat, and land that has remained in family stewardship for generations. E12
would not merely be visible from that property; it would aﬀect the creek environment and
the natural corridor that gives the property its character. This relates to the Commission’s
consideration of environmental integrity, historical and aesthetic values, and community
values, as it describes an existing creek-centered landscape rather than speculative future
plans. 26
         Seib’s testimony discusses existing natural resources and land uses along the
Salado Creek corridor. The Seib property includes creek frontage, heritage oaks, ranch
use, wildlife habitat, and community-oriented uses such as equine therapy. Link E12
would industrialize that setting with a permanent right-of-way, structure placement,
vegetation clearing, and long-term maintenance obligations. E12 would not simply cross
vacant rural acreage; it would alter a functioning creek and ranch landscape that already
serves environmental, family, agricultural, and community purposes. 27
         Bullock’s testimony adds a legacy dimension to the same environmental issues.
Her property includes live oaks, bluﬀs, cattle and wildlife uses, and land that has remained

        Holder’s testimony is one of the clearest parcel-speciﬁc examples. Her
approximately 24-acre family property is long and narrow, and E12 would run lengthwise
in a way that cuts through or along the property in the most disruptive manner. The route
would require removal of mature trees and privacy screening, including the live oaks that
separate the home from nearby roads and help deﬁne the property as a home. Holder’s
testimony shows a consequence of route geometry that is otherwise not captured by the
record: a carelessly placed line can, on a particular tract, needlessly divide and expose
a family property.29
        Cornett’s testimony shows that Tenroc Ranch is not simply undeveloped open
space. The Stewardship Award materials document the Cornetts’ restoration of rough,
overgrazed land into productive ranchland, including brush removal, rotational grazing,
water systems, creek improvements, wildlife preservation, and native grass restoration. 30
